parts.latex: Explain why the percentage of scores between 46 and 70 is twice your answer to part (a).
By using the values in the table above, find an approximate minimum score that a candidate would need to be placed in the top $10\%$ of the candidates.
parts.note: Top 10% score found from a z-table of normal probabilities, which is not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
Find the $z$-score of 70.

$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{70-58}{15} \\ &= 0.8 \end{aligned}$$

From the table, $P(Z<0.8)=0.7881$.

The area between the mean and $z=0.8$ is

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 0.7881-0.5 \\ &= 0.2881 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 28.81\%$$
criteria: Finds the $z$-score corresponding to 70, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score for 46 is $-0.8$.

By symmetry about the mean, the area between 46 and 58 equals the area between 58 and 70.

So the percentage of scores between 46 and 70 is twice $28.81\%$.

The top $10\%$ starts at the 90th percentile. From the table, $P(Z<1.3)\approx 0.9$, so $z=1.3$.

$$1.3=\dfrac{x-58}{15}$$

$$x=77.5$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Approximate minimum score}=77$$

Answers could include: 78
criteria: Correct answer, with evidence of using the table
Finds the $z$-score corresponding to the 90th percentile, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: normal distribution curve with 95% between 59 and 107

solutions.latex:
For a normal distribution, about $95\%$ of scores lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean. So the mean is the midpoint of 59 and 107.
$$\text{mean}=\dfrac{59+107}{2}=83$$
The distribution is symmetric, so the modal score equals the mean, $83$.

The distance from 59 to 107 is $4$ standard deviations.
$$\begin{aligned} 4\sigma &= 107-59 = 48 \\ \sigma &= 12 \end{aligned}$$
The range of a normal distribution is not given by the interval 59 to 107, so the range of $48$ in A and B is not correct.

Hence modal score $=83$ and standard deviation $=12$, which is option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following statements is true regarding data which is normally distributed?

solutions.latex:
A normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean $\mu$ (any real number) and standard deviation $\sigma>0$.

Option A is false: the mean can be any value, including zero (as in the standard normal distribution).

Option C is false: a normal distribution is symmetric, so it is not skewed.

Option D is false: a standard deviation is never negative.

Option B is true: if $\sigma = 0$ every value would be the same, and there would be no bell-shaped curve.
$$\therefore\ \text{option B}$$

meta.self_check: Each option checked against properties of the normal distribution; matches key B.

figures.cap: two normal curves A (mean 12, wider) and B (mean 15, narrower)

solutions.latex:
The mean is the value at the centre of each curve (the dashed lines).

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Curve A: mean} &= 12 \\ \text{Curve B: mean} &= 15 \end{aligned}$$
So curve B has the greater mean, by 3.

The standard deviation measures the spread of the scores about the mean. Curve A is wider and flatter, while curve B is narrower and taller.

Therefore curve A has the greater standard deviation.

$$\therefore\ \text{B has the greater mean, and A has the greater standard deviation.}$$

parts.latex: For a normally distributed set of scores, which of the following statements is FALSE?

solutions.latex:
For a normal distribution, a $z$-score greater than $2$ lies further into the tail than a $z$-score greater than $1$.

So it has a lower probability, not a higher one, and statement D is false.

Statements A, B and C are all true properties of a normal distribution.
